facts.text: The Moon is a ball of rock that makes no light of its own: it shines only because sunlight bounces off it. The Sun always lights the half of the Moon that faces it, and the half turned away is dark, at every phase. So the Moon itself never changes shape; only how much of its lit half we see changes. Earth is lit the same way: the half of Earth facing the Sun has day, and the other half has night. A lamp and a ball in a dark room model the phases part for part: the lamp stands for the Sun, the ball for the Moon, and your head for Earth. Hold the ball at arm's length and turn slowly in a circle. The ball makes no light of its own, and the lamp always lights the half of it facing the lamp. But as you turn, you see all, part or none of that lit half, so the bright part you see seems to grow and shrink.

The Moon orbits Earth, going all the way around about once a month, so its place around Earth keeps changing, and so does how much of its lit half faces Earth. The shape we see from Earth is called a phase, and it shows where the Moon is in its orbit. At new moon, the Moon is between Earth and the Sun: its lit half faces away from Earth, the side facing us is dark, and we cannot see it. From new moon to full moon the Moon is waxing: each night more of its lit half faces Earth, so the lit part we see grows. About a week after new moon, at first quarter, sunlight covers half of the face we see, like a half circle. About two weeks after new moon, at full moon, the Moon is on the far side of Earth from the Sun, and we see its whole lit half. From full moon back to new moon the Moon is waning: each night less of its lit half faces Earth, so the lit part we see shrinks. About three weeks after new moon, at third quarter, half of the face we see is lit again, the opposite half from first quarter. Between new moon and a quarter, the lit part looks like a thin crescent; between a quarter and full moon, it is more than half, called gibbous. The Moon takes the same path every orbit, so the phases always come in the same order (new moon, first quarter, full moon, third quarter and back to new moon), and the whole cycle repeats about every 29.5 days.

Anyone can watch the Moon's shape change from one night to the next just by looking up. Just after sunset, a thin crescent Moon can often be seen low in the sky near where the Sun went down, with its bright edge facing the Sun. Over the following nights its lit part grows into a half circle and then a full moon. The same side of the Moon always faces Earth, because the Moon spins once on its axis each time it goes around Earth, so there is a far side we never see from Earth. That far side is not always dark: at new moon, it is the half that is fully lit. A common mistake is thinking that Earth's shadow causes the phases. It does not. The phases come from how much of the Moon's sunlit half faces Earth, and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon only during a lunar eclipse.

A lunar eclipse can happen only at full moon. It happens when the Sun, Earth and the Moon line up exactly and Earth blocks the sunlight headed for the Moon, so Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees, so most months the full moon passes just above or below Earth's shadow and there is no eclipse. In a total lunar eclipse, the full moon goes dim and often turns a coppery red, because some sunlight bends through Earth's air and still reaches it. Within a few hours, the Moon moves out of Earth's shadow and is a bright full moon again. Eclipses are the next topic after the phases: an eclipse happens when the Sun, Earth and the Moon line up so that one of them blocks sunlight from reaching another and casts its shadow on it.

misconception: Many people think Earth's shadow causes the Moon's phases. In fact, the phases come from how much of the Moon's sunlit half faces Earth; Earth's shadow falls on the Moon only during a lunar eclipse, at full moon.

lesson_markdown:
# Why does the Moon change shape?

**If the Moon is a round ball, why does it look like a thin sliver on some nights and a full circle on others?**

The Moon never really changes shape. Sunlight always lights half the Moon; as the Moon orbits Earth, we see more or less of that half. The shapes we see are called **phases**, and each one shows where the Moon is in its orbit.

## Try it with a lamp and a ball

In a dark room, hold a ball at arm's length and turn slowly in a circle. The ball makes no light of its own, and the lamp always lights the half of it that faces the lamp. But as you turn, you see all of that lit half, part of it, or none of it. In this model, the lamp is the Sun, the ball is the Moon, and your head is Earth.

## Why the phases happen

1. **The Moon makes no light.** It is a ball of rock that shines only because sunlight bounces off it.
2. **Half is always lit.** The Sun lights the half of the Moon that faces it, and the half turned away is dark.
3. **The Moon moves.** It **orbits** Earth about once a month, so its place around Earth keeps changing.
4. **Our view changes.** From each new place, a different amount of the lit half faces Earth, so we see a different phase.
5. **The pattern repeats.** The Moon takes the same path every orbit, so the phases come in the same order about every 29.5 days.

You already know this idea from day and night: the half of Earth facing the Sun has day, and the other half has night.

## The phases in order

At **new moon**, the Moon is between Earth and the Sun. Its lit half faces away from Earth, so we can't see it.

So what do you think we see when the Moon is on the far side of Earth from the Sun? We see its whole lit half: that's the **full moon**.

| Phase | About when | What we see |
|---|---|---|
| New moon | Start of the cycle | None of the lit half |
| First quarter | A week after new moon | Half of the face lit |
| Full moon | Two weeks after new moon | The whole lit half |
| Third quarter | Three weeks after new moon | The opposite half of the face lit |

From new moon to full moon, more of the lit half faces Earth each night: that's **waxing**. From full moon back to new moon, less of it faces Earth each night: that's **waning**. In between, the lit part looks like a thin crescent or a more-than-half gibbous shape.

Here's a surprise: at new moon, the Moon's far side, the side we never see from Earth, is fully lit.

*Simplified: each step in the table takes about a week, not exactly a week.*

## A common mistake

Many people think Earth's shadow causes the phases. It doesn't: the phases come from how much of the Moon's sunlit half faces Earth. Earth's shadow falls on the Moon only during a lunar eclipse, which can happen only at full moon. Most months the full moon passes just above or below Earth's shadow, because the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees. Eclipses are the next topic in this unit.

## Check yourself

If the Sun always lights half the Moon, why can't we see the Moon at all at new moon?

Want to dig deeper? Ask a follow-up question!
